instructions: Answer all 40 questions. Listen to each recording ONCE. Read each question group during the pauses. Follow the word limit for completion questions. Transcripts and explanations are available only after submission.

parts.title: Choosing a sailing course
parts.context: A beginner asks a sailing-club adviser to compare introductory course options.

speakers.description: Adult prospective learner, natural Australian English.

script.text: Good morning, sailing course enquiries. I can help you compare the beginner options. Are you looking for a course yourself, or asking on behalf of a group? The choice depends partly on whether you want to try sailing for a day or begin a more structured course.

Just for myself. I've been reading the course information, but I'm not yet sure how much to commit to. I've enjoyed being near the water, although I've never actually learned to sail. I'd rather understand what each option involves before choosing. A friend may be interested later, but I don't want to book for somebody who hasn't decided.

Then the introductory day is worth considering. It gives someone with no experience a chance to see whether sailing is something they want to continue. A single place on the introductory day costs 120 pounds. That's the price for one person booking independently, rather than part of a pair.
I had another figure in mind. I think I saw a lower price when I was looking through the information. Was I looking at an old offer, or does it depend on when you go?

The lower figure concerns booking together. If two people book, the price is 110 pounds each. It's a reduction per person, not a total price for both. If your friend decides to join you, that distinction matters when you're comparing costs. You don't need previous experience for the introductory day.

That explains it. I wouldn't want to tell my friend the wrong total. Would we be joining a very large group? I know group activities can be enjoyable, but I also want a chance to ask questions rather than just watch from a distance.

The groups are small: eight would be usual, with ten as the maximum. Everyone is a beginner, so people are normally willing to ask basic questions. But if you already know you want to start learning systematically, the first-level course offers a clearer sequence of practical work and theory.

Is that spread over several weeks? I could attend a weekend more easily than a series of evenings. My work pattern varies, and promising to be available on the same evening every week would be difficult.

The first-level course lasts 2 days. Both are at the weekend, so it isn't a weekly evening commitment. It's a more substantial start than the introductory day, while still being a beginner course. Completing it also prepares you to move on to the next level rather than repeat an introduction.

I assumed I might have to wait until summer. Is that a seasonal restriction, or is it simply that summer is when most people think about taking up sailing? I don't want to confuse what is popular with what is actually available.

The weekend course runs throughout the year. You don't have to wait for a summer-only season. There is classroom learning as well as practical work, so don't imagine the course is only a matter of getting into a boat and hoping you understand what to do.
That sounds sensible. What does the classroom part cover? I can imagine learning names for parts of the boat, but I'm less sure what else a complete beginner needs to know before going out.

The theory includes weather, together with tides. Those are important to understanding the conditions in which you'll sail. The practical element takes you into the harbour in training dinghies. You share with another learner and an instructor, who explains the safety aspects as well as the sailing skills. Being a beginner is expected, so you aren't supposed to arrive knowing the terminology.

Good. The language is one thing I thought I might struggle with. I can follow an explanation if I can connect a new term to what I'm looking at, but a long list of unfamiliar words without pictures would be rather difficult.

There's help with that. A dictionary is included in the first-level course fee. It explains sailing terms with pictures, so you can return to a word after the instructor has introduced it. The course costs two hundred pounds, with a discount for club members. You can consider membership separately; you don't need to decide that simply to understand the course options.

And is there any record of completing the course? I don't mean a professional licence. I just want to know how the beginner level connects with whatever comes next, especially if I take a break before continuing.

At the end you receive a certificate. That marks completion of this course, after which the second-level course is the next step. It's useful to distinguish completing a beginner programme from being ready to do every kind of sailing independently. The course is a starting point, with instruction throughout.

Yes, that's what I meant. Before I choose, could we go through what I would need to bring? I can swim confidently, but I don't have specialist sailing clothing. I'd prefer to know which equipment is provided rather than buy things unnecessarily.

You do need to be able to swim. The club provides the wetsuit and life jacket. Bring swimming clothing and some old trainers yourself. You'll also need a towel. Toiletries such as shampoo are your own choice, but people generally appreciate having them after being on the water. Don't assume that because specialist equipment is supplied, ordinary personal items are included too.
I would certainly have forgotten at least one of those. What about food? I could carry lunch, although it would be easier if I could buy something rather than pack everything before setting off.

The club has a cafe. It sells sandwiches, cakes and other snacks, so there is a place to buy food and drink. That gives you an option; it doesn't mean the course is a catered holiday. When comparing the courses, keep the teaching and included equipment separate from whatever you choose to purchase to eat.

Understood. Is there something I can do beforehand so that the first explanation feels a little less unfamiliar? I wouldn't want to teach myself incorrectly, but seeing the setting before arriving might help.

The recommended preparation is to watch the training videos online. They introduce what to expect and make the first day less unfamiliar. They support the course rather than replace the instructor, so you shouldn't feel you need to master every skill from a screen before attending.

That would help. One last thing: I'll be travelling by bicycle, which means I may have a few personal items with me. I don't want to keep anything valuable in the boat or leave it loose while we're on the water.

There are lockers in the changing rooms. You can store valuables there while you take part. So, to recap the decision rather than book you immediately: the introductory day lets you try sailing, while the weekend course combines theory and practical skills and leads towards the next level. Think about which suits your aim, and whether your friend is genuinely ready to book as well.

parts.title: Entering film makeup work
parts.context: A makeup artist explains career preparation and everyday trainee duties in film production.

speakers.description: Adult careers speaker, natural New Zealand English.

script.text: Welcome. Today I will describe entering film makeup work through a trainee role. We will consider gaining experience, working with other people, building a portfolio and carrying out daily duties. A trainee role can sound glamorous when described only in terms of the finished film. We will look at the practical side, including routine work that audiences never see.

The route I am describing involves about two years of trainee work before becoming a film makeup artist. For someone seeking a first opportunity, a short film with a small budget may offer experience. However, we need to distinguish the chance to learn from the conditions under which the work happens. On a small-budget project, ensure transport expenses are covered. That isn't the same as promising a wage. Food is another separate consideration: trainees are told to bring supplies because catering may not be available. These distinctions matter when someone hears the word 'expenses' and imagines that every personal cost has been provided for.

A large production can offer a different range of experience. Hair and makeup are separate departments on such films. That means you shouldn't assume that being in the makeup department will automatically teach you a variety of hair styles. Nor should you expect immediate practical access to specialist effects work, which has its own expertise. One valuable opportunity is working with people from different ethnic backgrounds. There is also a range of ages. The benefit is breadth of experience with people, rather than a promise that a beginner will be assigned every specialist technique.

The working atmosphere can be demanding. Long empty hours are not the defining difficulty of the makeup department. Instead, there can be considerable pressure to keep working while responding professionally to other people. Directors may be impatient or dissatisfied with the result. An experienced makeup artist has to manage that interaction without losing control of the task. A trainee can learn from how a supervisor responds. That is different from learning only a technical procedure: professional conduct is visible in the response to an awkward situation as well as in the finished appearance.

Meeting well-known actors is another adjustment. I remember feeling so shy that conversation was difficult. It wasn't a feeling of pride in having reached the same status, and it wasn't disappointment that the actors looked different in person. Over time, meeting performers became an ordinary part of work. The useful distinction is between an initial emotional reaction and a continuing professional relationship. Treating a workplace meeting as an opportunity to seek personal photographs would miss the purpose of being there.

Now consider the trainee's kit. It needs to be available when a task arises, but that doesn't mean buying an elaborate collection of expensive products at the outset. The recommendation is a kit containing the essentials. A beginner may learn from observing what experienced colleagues carry, while respecting that somebody else's equipment is not automatically available to borrow. Looking carefully and asking permission are different actions. The required kit should match the tasks a trainee is actually expected to carry out, rather than an imagined role involving every specialist effect on a film.

A portfolio helps show the work a trainee has done. Photographs can show development across the stages of an application, rather than only a finished face. However, making a useful record does not remove the need for authorisation. Obtain approval from the makeup designer before using work photographs in the portfolio. Your portfolio can be sent digitally, so printing a complete collection is not the priority. Later I will mention printed continuity records. Those serve a different purpose, and the instruction about them should not be transferred automatically to a personal portfolio.

Let us move from career preparation to everyday duties. An actor may arrive with skin already cleansed and moisturised. When that preparation hasn't been done, a trainee may be asked to do it before the makeup artist starts. It has to happen quickly enough to avoid delaying the rest of the work. This is not an invitation to rush carelessly; it describes the need to complete a familiar supporting task efficiently within a schedule. Being prepared and understanding the next step help someone work at the required pace.

Another duty concerns continuity. Scenes may be filmed out of sequence, and a reshoot can happen much later. The makeup has to be reproduced, which makes reliable records important. Photographs are logged digitally and a printed copy is kept in the actor's file. Here the central requirement is organisation. If a record cannot be found when it is needed, taking it originally has done little good. Notice again the difference from the portfolio: the continuity record supports reproducing a particular appearance, while the portfolio presents work to others.

General duties may be far less specialised. They can include making drinks and putting washing on, not simply preparing an actor for the camera. The useful attitude here is flexibility: being ready to help with a range of requests. A trainee who treats every ordinary task as beneath them is misunderstanding the role being described. That doesn't mean confusing the work with independent responsibility for the entire department. It means recognising that supporting a production involves small practical contributions as well as opportunities to develop a craft.

Finally, we need to distinguish between principal cast members and extras. Trainees may apply makeup to extras, rather than taking charge of the principal cast. When many people need to be ready, pace matters again. Spending too long with each person can delay the group. Confidence develops through understanding the limited task, doing it competently and keeping the whole schedule in view. The overall picture is a combination of technical learning, reliable records, appropriate permission and professional behaviour. Together, they explain why a trainee's day involves much more than the most visible creative work.

parts.title: Evaluating marine-biodiversity resources
parts.context: Two students evaluate a marine-biodiversity lecture and resources for a seminar.

speakers.description: Adult student, natural North American English.

script.text: Before we choose material for the seminar, can we compare our notes on the visiting lecture? I'd read about ocean biodiversity before, so I wasn't starting with no knowledge. What stayed with me was the attention to long-term threats. Some aren't attracting much public attention yet, but that doesn't make them unimportant.

I agree. My first note says 'useful solutions', but looking back that isn't quite right. We were shown problems that may be difficult to solve, rather than a convenient action for every threat. The important change was looking further ahead. I should rewrite that note before I repeat it in the seminar.

There were suggestions about policy, though, particularly ways countries could protect marine and coastal environments. I don't want to imply that the speaker offered nothing practical. We need to separate what was included from what had the strongest effect on us. Something can be useful without being the reason a lecture changes your view.

The examples also showed how worldwide the threats are. The national policy points were one part, but the examples weren't restricted to a single country's coastline. That broader scale made a difference to my understanding. A local example might be easier to picture, but it wasn't the defining feature of this lecture.

Then there was the research team. I wrote down that some members had been warning about ocean pollution years earlier. It would be tempting to say the main strength was their record of previous work, because that's easy to put in a sentence. But that wasn't what I found most impressive about the project.

For me, it was the range of expertise in one team. People with very different backgrounds were contributing to the same investigation. Being international is useful, but remote collaboration isn't unusual in itself. The mix of specialisms was the point. We should explain why bringing those perspectives together mattered, rather than list the countries represented.

Yes. I also liked how the speaker handled numerical evidence. There were figures available, but she explained the general implications instead of filling the lecture with numbers. That helped me understand the argument without confusing the amount of data shown with the strength of the explanation.

And the technology was memorable. The description of robots used to investigate threats was especially interesting. Improved tracking systems were mentioned too. Those examples explained how researchers could find things out, rather than merely telling us to be impressed by a new device. Technology was connected to a research purpose.

That gives us an introduction. Now we need to be more critical about the reading and listening resources. I don't think 'interesting' is a sufficient judgment for every one. We have to say whether a resource explains its claims, fits our audience and gives a balanced account. Otherwise our seminar contribution will become a list of titles.

Let's start with the article on invasive lionfish. The claim was that their habitat was expanding through the Mediterranean. The writer described the environmental danger quite strongly. My first reaction was that forceful language meant it must be a convincing article, but I couldn't find enough support for the claims.

That's the same distinction I made. I wasn't dismissing the possibility of harm. The problem was the lack of evidence explaining the danger. We shouldn't criticise it for being too specialised; the language wasn't what prevented us evaluating the claim. It needed a clearer basis for the conclusions. In our notes, 'not sufficiently supported' is more accurate than simply 'wrong'.

Next, the documentary about microplastics. I started watching it and then noticed when it had been produced. I stopped because it was old. You watched the whole thing, didn't you? I wondered whether I'd been unfair to reject it before seeing the end.

I did finish it. Some explanations might help a complete beginner, but for our seminar it felt outdated. The account belonged to a stage when microplastics were much less familiar to the public. We need to be careful: its age doesn't prove that every statement is false. It means it doesn't give the current perspective our discussion needs. We can describe that limitation without inventing a scientific error we didn't actually identify.

The ocean-pollution podcast had a different weakness. It referred to pesticides and plastic and explained that they were harmful. I kept expecting it to go beyond the points we already knew. There wasn't much to challenge or extend our understanding.

I found it predictable too. That's different from saying it was too old or impossible to follow. It was easy enough to understand; it simply offered little beyond familiar points. We could mention it as a basic introduction, but we shouldn't present it as the most useful preparation for people who've already attended the lecture.

The book on coastal ecosystems was almost the reverse. Initially I thought it might be too detailed. It went into offshore wind farms and fish farms, which took more concentration than the podcast. But when I finished, the relationships between the issues were clearer. The diagrams helped me follow the explanation.

Me too. So we shouldn't equate difficulty at the beginning with failure overall. The detail and diagrams contributed to understanding. For this resource, a positive evaluation needs to say what became clearer, rather than only report that we enjoyed it. We can recommend selected sections and explain how the illustrations support the written discussion.

I can't make the same recommendation for the metal-toxicity article at our present level. It deals with metals from industrial emissions and reactions in the sea, but I couldn't follow the explanation. I kept rereading without getting a usable account of the process.

It seemed to expect specialist knowledge. That's an audience problem for us, rather than proof that the researchers are mistaken. We should avoid writing 'weak evidence' just because the argument was beyond our understanding. Our evaluation can say who the resource might suit and why we need a more accessible introduction first.

Finally, the floating-marine-cities podcast. I found the idea engaging, and the account of possible benefits to people was easy to follow. At first I thought that made it a good conclusion to our seminar. But then I noticed what was missing.

It gave a one-sided account. The environmental effects received little attention compared with the benefits for people. That matters in a seminar about biodiversity. An interesting proposal still needs its costs examined. We can use it to raise a question, as long as we don't treat the podcast's emphasis as a balanced evaluation.

So our notes need different reasons for different judgments: support for claims, age and relevance, new insight, clarity, assumed knowledge and balance. That should make the discussion more useful than putting each resource into a simple good-or-bad column. Let's organise the seminar around those distinctions, with one clear example for each.

parts.title: Examining sources of rubber
parts.context: A lecturer explains constraints on rubber production, threats to supply and alternative sources.

speakers.description: Adult lecturer, natural British English, steady academic pace.

script.text: Today we will examine the production and supply of rubber. The purpose is to understand a chain of explanation: what makes a material useful, why supply may be constrained, what can threaten that supply, and how an alternative source might address some limitations while introducing others. We will keep those questions separate. A material can be useful without being suitable for every application, and a plant can contain rubber without immediately becoming a practical replacement for existing production. We will use these examples to understand the different constraints on production.

Rubber belongs alongside metals and fossil fuels as an important material in an industrial economy. Metals provide structures and machinery, while fuels provide power. Rubber contributes flexible parts such as belts, pipes and components that absorb shocks. These are less visually prominent than a large machine, but they help connect parts and make systems function. The everyday range extends from footwear to medical gloves. This introduction is a reminder that the importance of a resource cannot be judged simply by how noticeable it is in a finished object.

Most natural rubber comes from the Para rubber tree. The tree originated in Brazil, although the plantations discussed are in South-East Asia. To obtain the material, workers make small cuts in the trunk and collect the liquid that emerges. The liquid collected from the tree is called latex. Collection is manual and labour-intensive. That matters because increasing output is not simply a matter of pressing a button on a machine: people and a suitable living crop are involved at several stages.

The first constraint is time. A planted tree may take 8 to 10 years before it begins producing. That is very different from changing the area devoted to an annual crop. Suppose demand rises after a farmer has made a planting decision. The long wait limits how quickly that decision can produce additional material. Conversely, if demand falls, a tree planted years earlier has not become a short-term crop that can easily be replaced. For our purposes, the key point is the delay between committing land and obtaining output.

Eight years is the lower end of that range, rather than a guaranteed wait for every tree. A range communicates uncertainty and variation; replacing it with one exact promise would misrepresent how the crop develops. This is also why a long production cycle is connected to demand. The problem is not simply that trees grow slowly in an abstract sense. It is that producers must make decisions well before they know precisely what the market will require.

Location imposes another constraint. The tree needs an appropriate combination of rainfall, temperature and altitude. We can group those requirements under suitable climate, while remembering that height above sea level also affects growing conditions. Having land available somewhere does not mean it is suitable land for this particular crop. Production is concentrated close to the equator. We cannot assume that the same trees can simply be moved into any northern or southern region when extra supply is needed. Geography and the long lead time therefore limit different aspects of expansion.

There is also a problem after manufacture and use. Some materials can return relatively easily to a production cycle. Rubber is difficult to recycle. Notice the wording: difficult does not mean impossible. Comparing this difficulty with more familiar recycling streams explains why recovering used material cannot be assumed to solve a shortage. This is a useful example of how an absolute statement can distort an argument. If we write that rubber can never be recovered, we have made a much stronger claim than the evidence supports.

Now turn from long-standing production constraints to threats. The plantations we are discussing derive from a small number of seeds taken from Brazil during the nineteenth century. That restricted starting population means low genetic diversity. When many trees are closely related, a disease to which they are susceptible can threaten a large share of the crop. This is a biological vulnerability, not the same thing as slow growth. Even if a tree has reached productive age, its relationship to the wider population may still make supply vulnerable to a shared disease.

A fungus presents a particularly serious disease threat. Damage to Brazilian rubber trees illustrates the potential consequence for plantations elsewhere. We should preserve that distinction between an observed example and a wider potential risk. That does not mean every plantation has already suffered the same event. The underlying reasoning is that a population with little variation may have limited resilience when a relevant disease arrives. A dramatic example needs to be connected to that mechanism, rather than used as a substitute for explaining it.

A different pressure comes from farmers' choices. Farmers may move towards palm oil because it may be easier and more profitable to cultivate. This is an economic competition for land and labour, rather than a disease of the rubber tree. Extreme weather is a further threat, again with a different mechanism. It is tempting to put every pressure under one heading such as environmental change, but doing so can hide why an intervention might address one problem and leave another untouched. Better disease resistance would not by itself remove an incentive to grow a more profitable crop.

What about synthetic rubber? It is useful for certain engine components and cooking equipment, so the comparison is not a choice between a universally useful natural material and a useless manufactured one. The limitation concerns properties needed for particular applications. The strength required in demanding uses, including aircraft tyres, limits the extent to which synthetic material can replace natural rubber. The important point is that materials must be compared against the demands of a particular application. A tyre formulation is an engineering decision; our concern is the argument that one substitute may serve some functions without replacing the original in all of them.

That explains the search for another biological source of natural rubber. The example is a type of dandelion. The familiar yellow flower may seem an unlikely industrial resource, but rubber is found in its roots. The relevant part is below the ground, so recognising the flower does not identify where the material is extracted. There is also a limitation: compared with the tree, the plant yields relatively small amounts. An alternative is not established by mentioning only its most attractive feature and omitting the scale of what it produces.

The attraction is adaptability. These dandelions can grow in many locations and do not require rich soil. That contrasts with the tree's more restrictive growing conditions. It suggests why researchers would investigate the plant, not why every supply difficulty has already been solved. Yield and cultivation possibilities need to be considered together. The final lesson is therefore about comparing constraints: the tree's delayed production, suitable growing region, labour requirements and biological vulnerability; the limits of recycling and substitution; and the trade-off between a potential alternative's adaptability and its smaller output.
